procedural_history.originating_court: A lower court granted bail to Accused No. 1.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 16.03.2022 passed by the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amravati in Criminal Petition No. 788 of 2022.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Central Bureau of Investigation (C.B.I.) filed Criminal Petition No. 788 of 2022 before the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amaravati under Section 439(2) Cr.P.C. seeking cancellation of bail granted to Accused No. 1. The High Court dismissed the petition, holding that once Accused No. 1 was released on default bail under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C., the bail could not be cancelled on merits.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The C.B.I., feeling aggrieved by the High Court's judgment and order refusing to cancel the bail, preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court (Criminal Appeal No. 37 of 2023). The C.B.I. prayed to allow the appeal and cancel the bail granted to Accused No. 1, considering the chargesheet, the seriousness of the offenses, and the gravity of the offenses.

issue.issue_text: Whether the bail granted under the proviso to sub-section (2) of Section 167 Cr.P.C. for failure to complete the investigation within the prescribed period can be cancelled after the presentation of a chargesheet, and if so, on what grounds and circumstances?

facts: The issue concerns an accused person who was granted 'default bail' under the proviso to Section 167(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
This type of bail is granted when the investigating agency fails to complete its investigation and file a chargesheet within the prescribed time limit.
After the accused was released, the investigating agency completed the investigation and filed a chargesheet.
The prosecution then sought to have the default bail cancelled.
law: The Court established that bail granted under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C. is legally 'deemed' to be bail granted under Chapter XXXIII of the Cr.P.C.
Chapter XXXIII contains Sections 437(5) and 439(2), which explicitly grant courts the power to cancel bail.
Therefore, a legal mechanism exists to cancel default bail, just like any other bail granted under Chapter XXXIII.
application: The Court reasoned that an accused released on default bail does not acquire a special or absolute right to remain on bail indefinitely.
The initial release was based on a procedural failure by the prosecution (delay), not on an evaluation of the case's merits.
Once the chargesheet is filed, the court can consider the merits of the case.
However, the Court strongly emphasized that the mere filing of a chargesheet is not a sufficient ground for cancellation.
To cancel the bail, the prosecution must demonstrate 'special and strong grounds' that arise from the evidence presented in the chargesheet.
This involves showing that the chargesheet reveals the commission of a serious, non-bailable offence and that it is necessary to arrest the accused and commit them to custody.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that default bail granted under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C. can be cancelled after a chargesheet is filed. However, the cancellation is not automatic. It can only be done if the prosecution makes out a special and strong case, based on the contents of the chargesheet, showing that the accused has committed a serious non-bailable offence, thereby justifying their re-arrest and custody.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the bail granted under the proviso to sub-section (2) of Section 167 Cr.P.C. for failure to complete the investigation within the prescribed period can be cancelled after the presentation of a chargesheet, and if so, on what grounds and circumstances?
appellant_arguments: Since the bail was granted due to the default of the investigating agency and without the court adverting to the merits of the case, the merits brought about in the chargesheet and other attending circumstances become relevant for cancellation.
The bail should be cancelled on merits, considering the seriousness and gravity of the offences alleged to have been committed by the accused as detailed in the chargesheet.
The appellant also tried to make submissions on the post-bail conduct of the respondent as a ground for cancellation.
respondent_arguments: As per a catena of decisions of the Supreme Court, an accused is to be released on bail for the non-filing of a chargesheet within the prescribed period.
The respondent relied on the decision in the case of Mohamed Iqbal Madar Sheikh and Ors. to support their position.

cases.case_name: Aslam Babalal Desai Vs. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: For the observations made in the concurring judgment of Justice K. Ramaswamy (in paragraphs 39 and 40) and the dissenting judgment of Justice M.M. Punchhi (in paragraphs 23, 25, 26, 27 and 28).

cases.principle: For the observations and holdings in paragraphs 13 and 14 of the judgment, which were made after considering the decision in Aslam Babalal Desai.

cases.case_name: Raghubir Singh and Ors. Vs. State of Bihar
cases.principle: As a precedent on the law of bail that was followed by subsequent decisions.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The purpose of statutory interpretation is to sustain the law, and a court must interpret the language in a statute to promote public good and interdict the misuse of power.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A bail granted by default under the proviso to Section 167(2) Cr.P.C. is not a bail on merits. Consequently, after the chargesheet is filed, the court has the power to cancel this default bail by examining the merits of the case, such as the gravity of the offense and the evidence presented, to ensure justice is administered and to avoid rewarding investigative lethargy or potential collusion.
legal_tests_applied: Once a chargesheet is filed after an accused has been released on default bail, the prosecution may seek cancellation on the ground that there are 'very strong grounds' and 'reasonable grounds to believe that the accused has committed a non-bailable offence and that it is necessary to arrest him and commit him to custody.'
why_respondent_won: The court rejected the respondent's argument that default bail cannot be cancelled on merits, finding that such bail is not an order on merits but an order on the default of the prosecuting agency.

Accepting the respondent's view would give 'a premium to the lethargic and/or negligence' of the investigating agency, and potentially reward a 'deliberate attempt' not to file the chargesheet in time.

To say the court is 'for ever shut to see to the merits of the case, though it otherwise has power to cancel bail, is to deprive it of its elementary function to administer justice and weigh the claims on merit inter se.'

The occasion to grant or refuse bail on merit becomes available to the court only after the filing of the chargesheet, because 'earlier thereto merit of bail could not figure at the time of the grant of compulsive bail.'

A contrary interpretation 'would frustrate justice' if, after the filing of a chargesheet that makes out a strong case for a serious, non-bailable crime, the court could not cancel the bail and commit the person to custody.
policy_considerations: A bail order under Section 167(2) of the Code could be 'managed through a convenient investigating officer, however heinous be the crime,' and the court must have the power to later examine the merits to prevent abuse.
The court must interpret the law to 'promote public good and misuse of power is interdicted' and to avoid an interpretation that would 'frustrate justice.'
The goal of the court is to 'strike a judicial balance' between the 'claims of personal liberty and the larger interests of the State.'

Allowing cancellation on merits prevents giving a 'premium to illegality and/or dishonesty' where an accused, despite having committed a very serious offence, secures release through a delay in filing the chargesheet.
